Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Arun Patel was thirty-two years old and had worked as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel in Chicago for nearly six years. It was steady work, cleaning guest rooms and public areas, a job that required him to be invisible, efficient, and alone for long stretches. That aloneness had always felt neutral, even comfortable. That changed on a November night after his shift ended at eleven. He was walking through the employee parking lot, a gravel expanse behind the hotel’s kitchen, when a man stepped out from between two parked vans. The man was young, maybe early twenties, and he moved fast. Before Arun could react, the man grabbed Arun’s left arm, twisting it behind his back, and pressed something hard and sharp into his ribs on the right side. A knife. Arun could feel the point through his uniform shirt, just below his ribcage. The man said something, but Arun’s mind went white. He fumbled for his wallet, handed it over. Then the man punched him hard in the stomach, doubling him over, and ran. Arun sat on the cold gravel for what felt like a long time, one hand pressed to his ribs, the other clutching his empty pocket.

In the months that followed, Arun found that the memory of that night returned with a clarity that felt almost like reliving it. He could see the man’s jacket, the pattern of the gravel, the exact angle of the streetlight. But the clearest part was the physical sensation. Whenever something reminded him—a sudden movement in his peripheral vision, the sound of footsteps behind him, even the smell of the hotel’s kitchen grease—he would feel a sharp, stabbing pain in his right side, exactly where the knife had pressed. The left arm would ache, as if still twisted. His stomach would clench. He knew what had happened, could replay it in his mind in perfect detail, but when his wife, Priya, asked him to describe it, he found himself unable. The words would not come. He would open his mouth and nothing would form, as if the memory was locked behind a door that had no handle.

Arun had always been a fairly trusting person. He believed in giving people the benefit of the doubt. After the mugging, that belief crumbled. He began to see threat everywhere. The world felt like a stage where anyone—a guest checking in, a delivery driver, a colleague he’d known for years—could turn dangerous without warning. People were not what they seemed, he decided. They were hiding intentions, waiting for an opportunity. He trusted no one, least of all strangers. This conviction grew stronger each time he had to enter a hotel room to clean. Every closed door felt like an ambush. He started knocking and waiting longer before entering, listening for footsteps. He began to avoid certain tasks: cleaning the parking lot, taking out trash at night, working the late shift. He traded shifts with a coworker, which cost him a small favor and ate into his sleep because he now had to work early mornings instead. His supervisor noticed he was slower, more hesitant, but Arun could not explain why. When Priya asked why he seemed so jumpy, he said nothing. He could not find the words, and even if he could, he was not sure she would believe him. He had begun to feel that everyone, including her, was capable of turning on him.

The avoidance spread. He stopped walking to the drugstore after dark. He stopped taking the train if there were fewer than three other people in the car. He began to check the locks on their apartment three times before bed. Priya grew frustrated. She said he was becoming a different person, distant and irritable. He knew she was right, but he could not stop. What frightened him most was not the memory itself but the certainty that the next attack was only a matter of time. He scanned every face, every shadow. The world was a dangerous place, and he was not strong enough to survive again.

It was Priya who finally convinced him to see a doctor, after he flinched violently when she touched his arm from behind. He agreed mostly because he was exhausted. He had not had a full night’s sleep in weeks. The pain in his side came and went unpredictably. He hoped someone could tell him how to stop feeling like a target. He was afraid of never being able to trust anyone again—and more than that, he was afraid of what that mistrust was doing to his marriage, his job, his life. He came to the clinic not sure if talking would help, but certain that staying silent was no longer possible.
